newsitem.title: USA: Boeing considers new stretch version of 737.
newsitem.headline: Boeing considers new stretch version of 737.

text.p: Boeing Co. is considering a fourth version of its new-generation 737 model that would include slightly more capacity for some carriers, a company spokeswoman said on Friday.
The new version of the world's most widely used commercial jetliner, likely to be known as the 737-900, would not enter service until late 2000 or early 2001, company spokeswoman Susan Davis said.
Boeing commercial airplane group President Ron Woodward told The News Tribune in Tacoma the company likely would go ahead with the new derivative.
The new plane would extend the body of the 737-800 by about eight feet, allowing 18 additional seats in three rows.
The maximum capacity of the plane would remain the same at 189 passengers due to regulations requiring that airlines be able to evacuate the plane quickly.
But many carriers could get more passengers into the new jet because they fly with more than the minimum "seat pitch," allowing slightly more legroom in each row.
"For those airlines that fly with more seat pitch, this would accommodate them," Davis said.
She said the cost of developing the new derivative would be relatively low because no changes would be required other than two small added fuselage sections.
Woodard told The News Tribune the new 737 version was needed to compete with Airbus Industrie's A321 model, which can carry 185 in two classes or 199 in one class.

Boeing already is developing three new versions of the 737, including the midsized 737-700 and the smaller 737-600, which fly higher and faster than the current generation. Initial delivery of the 737-700 to launch customer Southwest Airlines is expected in October 1997.
Ireland's Aer Lingus and China Airlines are believed to be interested in the proposed new stretch model, the newspaper said.
